proposed_title: EPA Withdrew Its Disinfectant Enforcement Complaint Against GEO Group
proposed_description_short: EPA withdrew its complaint alleging GEO Group misused a disinfectant at an ICE facility; the docket gives no reason, so lobbying cannot be treated as the cause.
proposed_description_medium: EPA’s administrative docket identifies a Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act complaint against GEO Group concerning disinfectant use at its Adelanto, California, ICE facility. The agency withdrew the complaint in June 2025. ProPublica reported that EPA gave no explanation. The record supports the withdrawal and underlying allegations, not a causal link between lobbying and the decision.
proposed_description_long: The EPA’s administrative docket for The GEO Group, Inc. lists a Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act complaint filed in June 2024 and a withdrawal filing in June 2025. ProPublica reported that the case concerned GEO Group’s use of the disinfectant Halt at its Adelanto, California, immigration detention facility. According to the EPA complaint as summarized in that report, GEO employees used the product without the protective equipment required by its label on more than 1,000 occasions in 2022 and 2023; these were agency allegations, not findings established in the withdrawn case. The EPA docket lists the complaint as withdrawn and closed, while ProPublica reported that the withdrawal notice gave no explanation. GEO Group’s political contributions and lobbying may be relevant context, but the available record does not establish that they caused the EPA’s action or that the company received a favor in exchange. The title is therefore limited to the procedural outcome and the specific case subject.

proposed_title: Army Takes Soldier for Life Accounts Offline After Duckworth Tribute Post
proposed_description_short: Soldier for Life’s social accounts went offline after a post honoring Sen. Tammy Duckworth; sources gave different explanations.
proposed_description_medium: The Hill reported that Soldier for Life’s social media accounts went offline after the Army unit posted a tribute to Sen. Tammy Duckworth. A Defense Department source attributed the shutdown to backlash; an Army spokesperson cited a policy to deactivate accounts lacking qualified public-affairs staff. The timing is reported, but the sources do not establish that the post alone caused the shutdown.
proposed_description_long: The Hill reported that the Army’s Soldier for Life accounts went offline after the unit posted a tribute to Sen. Tammy Duckworth, a retired Army lieutenant colonel and Iraq War veteran. A Defense Department source familiar with the Army’s reasoning told the outlet that Secretary Dan Driscoll directed the profiles to be shut down following negative reactions to the tribute. An Army spokesperson gave a different explanation: the account was a legacy profile not directly managed by qualified Army personnel, and policy required accounts without designated public-affairs staff to be deactivated and archived. The article describes a December 12 memo limiting official Army social accounts and setting a deadline for unstaffed accounts. These statements support an account of the post, offline profiles and competing explanations. They do not resolve which reason controlled, whether the post alone triggered the decision, or when every profile was restored. The corrected title states the sequence without asserting a proven single cause.

proposed_title: Trump SoHo Buyers Alleged Developers Overstated Condominium Sales
proposed_description_short: A 2010 lawsuit alleged Trump SoHo marketers overstated sales; the complaint said buyers were told 30–60% of units had sold while filings showed 62 of 391.
proposed_description_medium: Buyers sued the Trump SoHo developers in federal court in August 2010, alleging that marketing statements overstated condominium sales. The complaint said project representatives told buyers and the press that roughly 30–60% of units had sold, while a later offering-plan filing reported 62 of 391 units sold, about 16%. Reuters summarized the allegations at filing. These are claims in a civil complaint, not a finding that Donald Trump committed fraud.
proposed_description_long: In August 2010, buyers of units in the Trump SoHo hotel-condominium project filed a civil complaint in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York. The complaint alleged that project representatives told prospective purchasers and the press that 30, 40, 50 or 60 percent of the units had sold, encouraging buyers to complete their purchases. It cited a later amendment to the offering plan reporting that 62 of 391 units had been sold, roughly 16 percent. Reuters reported the lawsuit when it was filed and likewise described the sales figures as allegations by the plaintiffs. The court filing supports what buyers claimed and the numbers they cited; it does not by itself establish that the defendants knowingly misled purchasers or that a court found fraud. The supplied New York Times link is about Trump’s 2024 criminal verdict, not this development or lawsuit. The packet also contains an allegation about a Manhattan district attorney inquiry and a campaign donation, but no relevant complaint, official disposition or contemporaneous source; that claim is left out rather than presented as fact.

proposed_title: Wisconsin GOP Said It Trained More Than 5,000 Election Observers for 2024
proposed_description_short: Reuters reported that the RNC and Wisconsin Republican Party said they trained more than 5,000 election observers in Wisconsin.
proposed_description_medium: Reuters reported on October 31, 2024, that the Republican National Committee and Republican Party of Wisconsin said they had trained more than 5,000 election observers in the state. The report also described separate grassroots groups planning to deploy observers and monitor ballot drop boxes. It does not establish that Trump personally directed the training or that the program was a statewide voter-intimidation operation.
proposed_description_long: In an October 31, 2024 report about election observers in Wisconsin, Reuters said the Republican National Committee and Republican Party of Wisconsin reported training more than 5,000 observers. The article separately described grassroots groups that planned to deploy up to 1,500 observers collectively at voting sites and count centers and to monitor ballot drop boxes. It also reported local election officials’ concerns about observer conduct during earlier absentee-ballot processing in Milwaukee-area communities. Those facts support reporting on party training and local organizing, with attribution to the groups and officials. They do not show that Donald Trump personally deployed the observers, establish a nationwide strategy, or prove that all observers engaged in intimidation. The original headline combines separate actors and allegations into a single claim that the source does not establish. The replacement title focuses on the verifiable training statement, while the description keeps the other plans attributed and the claimed national intent unresolved.

proposed_title: Yosemite Ranger Shannon Joslin Fired After Hanging Transgender Pride Flag
proposed_description_short: AP reports Yosemite ranger Shannon “SJ” Joslin was fired after hanging a transgender pride flag; this single case does not establish a broader pattern.
proposed_description_medium: The AP reports that Yosemite ranger and biologist Shannon “SJ” Joslin was fired after helping hang a large transgender pride flag on El Capitan in May 2025. The termination letter cited unacceptable conduct and the flag incident; Joslin said the display was in a personal capacity. The article documents one case, not a pattern across federal agencies.
proposed_description_long: The Associated Press reports that Yosemite National Park ranger and biologist Shannon “SJ” Joslin was fired after hanging a large transgender pride flag on El Capitan in May 2025. AP says Joslin and other climbers displayed the flag for about two hours and removed it voluntarily. A termination letter cited failure to demonstrate acceptable conduct in Joslin’s role as a biologist and referred to the May incident; Joslin said the action was taken as a private citizen. The article also reports that other Yosemite employees were placed on administrative leave while the park investigated. These details support a focused account of Joslin’s firing and the stated basis in the termination letter, with the employee’s characterization separately attributed. The article does not establish that federal agencies broadly fired transgender employees or workers who supported trans rights, nor does it document the additional examples in the broader original title. Narrowing the title to the AP-documented Yosemite case keeps the entry within the evidence. Any broader pattern would require separate agency records and case-specific reporting.
